newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australian October imports.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW - Australian October imports.

text.p: Australian merchandise imports were rose 1.0 percent in October, according to official figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
Economists' median forecasts had centred on a 0.5 percent rise in imports. Forecasts had ranged from a 2.0 percent fall to a 4.0 percent rise.
A selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data follow.
TIM PFITZNER, ECONOMIST, NATIONAL AUSTRALIA BANK

"It looks like overall imports are rebounding a little bit. There's been a couple of months of pluses now. It looks like it's mostly in intermediate goods and capital goods, which we've been keeping a pretty close eye on, actually fell quite substantially again this month. (As a result), we're a bit concerned about business investment here just given the partial numbers."

"The fact that the consumption and the capital goods imports were down, offset by a rise in intermediate, is indicative that demand still remains pretty slack in the economy for both investment goods which ought to be showing up in the capital goods imports and also finished consumption goods. It is telling us the economy is still pretty weak, so I guess it yet again calls into question the government's three and a half percent growth forecast. So if anything, I see it as slightly positive for interest rate markets. Certainly, I don't think this is enough information to suggest that the Reserve Bank will cut again, but in terms of the balance these are more numbers showing the weakness in the economy, so if anything it should give some credence to the bulls in the market."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"It's a very bland number. It's broadly consistent with the economy ticking along. Domestic demand is growing to hold imports at reasonable sort of levels. We're in a range of A$1.3-1.7 billion for the current account deficit and this is going to be much the same on today's figures."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, UBS AUSTRALIA:

"It's continuing to creep up on the imports side. We reached the low point in July and we have had three months of increases now, so it is consistent with the current account deficit at the end of month somewhere in the A$1.7-1.8 billion compared to the A$1.2-1.3 billion we had towards mid-year. It doesn't give us a lot of clues, but it doesn't suggest undue weakness in the economy."
BRUCE HOCKMAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:

"I don't know that you can read an awful lot into it. If you really wanted to stretch things you might look at the capital goods imports. The big concerns is that we have seen that weaken in three out of four months, but given that growth wasn't expected to be in plant and equipment investment, it was (rather) non-dwelling construction, I don't think it has any great policy implications."
